lessons.title: Polite requests and responses at home
lessons.objective: Make polite requests, respond politely and address family members and visitors appropriately.
lessons.course:
Polite requests use soft words: “Could you pass me the salt, please?” “May I go out to play?” “Would you like some water?”
Polite responses: “Yes, of course.” “Here you are.” “No, thank you.” “I’m sorry, I can’t.”
We address people with the right title (Papa, Mama, Uncle, Auntie, Sir, Madam), we listen attentively and speak in turns.

support.title: Practise with the adult
support.text:
Could you help me carry the bucket, please?
Yes, of course. Here you are.
Thank you very much.

lessons.model: At dinner, Enow says: “Mama, could you pass me the plantains, please?” Mama answers: “Here you are, Enow.” Enow says: “Thank you, Mama.”
lessons.guided: Act five situations at home (asking for water, permission to go out, help with homework, offering a seat, refusing a second plate politely).
lessons.exercise: You want to go out to play. How do you ask Papa politely?
lessons.answer: May I go out to play, please?
accept: May I go out to play, please
May I go out to play
Can I go out to play, please
Could I go out to play, please
May I go out to play, please?
lessons.remediation: Learn two magic words first: “please” and “thank you”, then add “May I…?”.
lessons.transfer: Use “Could you…, please?” and “May I…?” at home all week.

practice.prompt: Match each request with a polite response.
practice.answer: water: Yes, please; salt: Here you are; come: I’m sorry, I can’t.

practice.prompt: Which request is the most polite?
Listen and answer politely.
practice.listen: Would you like some more rice?

lessons.title: Reading aloud: a description of our compound
lessons.objective: Read a short descriptive text aloud with correct intonation, reading sight words and multisyllabic words fluently.
lessons.course:
Before reading aloud, we look at long words and cut them into syllables: com-pound, ve-ran-dah, a-vo-ca-do, com-fort-a-ble.
We read groups of words together, we stop at full stops and pause at commas, and we read at a speed people can follow.

support.title: Read aloud
support.text: Our compound is quiet and comfortable. In front of the house there is a wide verandah where Grandpa rests in the afternoon. Behind the kitchen, an avocado tree gives us shade. Every Saturday, the children sweep the yard and water the flowers.

lessons.model: The adult reads the text, pausing at commas and stopping at full stops, then reads the long words syllable by syllable.
lessons.guided: Clap the syllables of five long words in the text. Read the text aloud three times, a little faster each time.
lessons.exercise: How many syllables are there in “avocado”?
lessons.remediation: Read one sentence at a time with the adult before reading the whole text.
lessons.transfer: Read a description of your own compound aloud to your family.

practice.prompt: Put the syllables in order.
Where does Grandpa rest in the afternoon?
practice.explanation: The text says he rests on the verandah.

practice.prompt: Listen to the text and read it aloud.
practice.listen: Our compound is quiet and comfortable. In front of the house there is a wide verandah where Grandpa rests in the afternoon.
practice.answer: The text read aloud with good pauses.
practice.explanation: Pause at commas, stop at full stops.

lessons.title: A descriptive essay: my home
lessons.objective: Write a descriptive essay of about 60 words about one’s home, with an introduction, a body and a conclusion.
lessons.course:
A descriptive essay paints a picture with words. Plan it in three parts:
• Introduction: say what you will describe (“I live in a small house in Mutengene.”).
• Body: describe the rooms, the colours, the people, the sounds and the smells.
• Conclusion: say how you feel about it (“I love my home because…”).
Use adjectives (bright, narrow, cosy) and connecting words (first, next, also).
lessons.model: The adult writes an introduction aloud: “My home is a brown house with a red roof near the main road.” Then adds two describing sentences.
lessons.guided: Make a plan with three boxes. Write the introduction, three sentences for the body, and one conclusion. Count your words.
lessons.exercise: Which part of an essay says how you feel about the subject at the end?
lessons.remediation: Write three sentences first: one for each part.
lessons.transfer: Read your essay to your family and ask them to add one detail.
lessons.materials: Paper, pencil, a plan with three boxes.

practice.prompt: Put the parts of an essay in order.
Which sentence is the best introduction?
choices: I live in a blue house near the market.
That is why I love it.
practice.answer: I live in a blue house near the market.
practice.explanation: The introduction says what you will describe.

practice.prompt: Write your descriptive essay: my home (about 60 words).
practice.answer: A descriptive essay of about 60 words with three parts.

lessons.title: Nouns: common, concrete and abstract; countable and uncountable
lessons.objective: Identify common, concrete and abstract nouns and use countable and uncountable nouns correctly.
lessons.course:
A concrete noun names something we can see or touch: table, mother, rice. An abstract noun names an idea or a feeling we cannot touch: love, joy, peace, honesty.
Countable nouns can be counted: one chair, two chairs. Uncountable nouns cannot be counted with numbers: water, rice, sugar, furniture. We say “much water, some rice, a cup of sugar”.
Plurals: add s (books), es (boxes, dishes), y → ies (baby → babies).
lessons.model: The adult points: “This cup is concrete. The love in our family is abstract.” Then: “one spoon, two spoons, but some salt.”
lessons.guided: Sort twelve words into concrete and abstract. Then put “a”, “an” or “some” before eight nouns.
lessons.exercise: Is “happiness” a concrete or an abstract noun?
lessons.remediation: Ask: Can I touch it? If yes, it is concrete.
lessons.transfer: Find five concrete nouns and two abstract nouns in a conversation at home.

practice.prompt: Match each noun with its kind.
practice.explanation: We can touch a chair, not kindness.

practice.prompt: Complete with the plural.
practice.text: one box, two [[boxes]]; one baby, three [[babies]]; one dish, four [[dishes]]
practice.explanation: es after x and sh; y → ies.

practice.prompt: Which one is uncountable?

lessons.title: Equal and equivalent sets at home
lessons.objective: Distinguish equal sets from equivalent sets and use the symbols = and ↔.
lessons.course:
Two sets are equal when they have exactly the same elements: {cup, plate} = {plate, cup}.
Two sets are equivalent when they have the same number of elements, even if the elements are different: {cup, plate, spoon} ↔ {mother, father, baby} (3 elements each).
All equal sets are equivalent, but equivalent sets are not always equal.
lessons.model: The adult places 3 spoons and 3 forks: “Same number: equivalent. Not the same things: not equal.”
lessons.guided: Make pairs of sets with objects from home. Say whether they are equal, equivalent or neither.
lessons.exercise: A = {bed, chair, table} and B = {pot, cup, plate}. Are A and B equal or equivalent?
lessons.remediation: Count the elements of each set first, then compare the elements themselves.
lessons.transfer: Find two equivalent sets in your kitchen.

practice.prompt: {3, 5, 7} and {7, 3, 5}: what are these sets?
A set has 6 elements. How many elements must an equivalent set have?
practice.explanation: Equivalent sets have the same number of elements.

practice.prompt: Match each pair with its relation.
practice.explanation: Compare elements, then the number of elements.

lessons.title: Numbers up to 5 000: reading, writing and place value
lessons.objective: Read, write and decompose four-digit numbers up to 5 000 using thousands, hundreds, tens and units.
lessons.course:
In 3 472: 3 thousands, 4 hundreds, 7 tens, 2 units. 3 472 = 3 000 + 400 + 70 + 2. We read: three thousand, four hundred and seventy-two.
To compare, look at the thousands first, then the hundreds: 3 472 > 3 427.
lessons.model: The adult writes 2 506 in a place-value table (Th H T U) and reads it: two thousand, five hundred and six.
lessons.guided: Write ten numbers in a place-value table. Decompose them and compare pairs with < or >.
lessons.exercise: What is the value of the digit 4 in 4 316?
lessons.remediation: Build numbers with bundles: 1 thousand = 10 hundreds.
lessons.transfer: Read the price of a bag of rice or of school fees in thousands.

practice.prompt: Write 2 000 + 300 + 50 + 9 as one number.
Which number is the greatest?
How many hundreds are there in 1 000?

lessons.title: The metric system: mm, cm, dm, m and km
lessons.objective: Establish the relationship between metric units of length and convert from one unit to another.
lessons.course:
1 cm = 10 mm; 1 dm = 10 cm; 1 m = 10 dm = 100 cm; 1 km = 1 000 m.
To change a big unit into a smaller one, multiply: 3 m = 300 cm. To change a small unit into a bigger one, divide: 4 000 m = 4 km.
lessons.model: The adult measures a table: “It is 1 m 20 cm long, that is 120 cm.”
lessons.guided: Measure five objects at home in cm, then write their length in m and cm, or in mm.
lessons.exercise: How many centimetres are there in 2 m?
lessons.remediation: Use a ruler to see 10 mm in 1 cm before converting.
lessons.transfer: Measure the length of your room in metres and centimetres.

practice.prompt: Convert 5 km into metres.
Match the equal lengths.
The door is 2 m 10 cm high. How many cm is that?

lessons.title: Tallying household items in 10s and 20s
lessons.objective: Collect data, tally in groups and represent the totals in a table.
lessons.course:
To count many things quickly, we tally: four strokes and a fifth across make a group of 5. Two groups make 10; four groups make 20.
We write the totals in a table with a title and two columns (item, number).
lessons.model: The adult tallies the cups, plates and spoons of the kitchen and counts the groups of 5.
lessons.guided: Tally three kinds of objects at home. Make a table of totals and say which is the most numerous.
lessons.exercise: How many is four complete groups of five tally marks?
lessons.transfer: Tally the visitors to your home during one week.

practice.prompt: How many tally marks show 35 in groups of 5? How many groups?
Which group of tally marks shows 5?
practice.explanation: The fifth stroke crosses the four.

practice.prompt: Draw your tally table of three household items.
practice.answer: A table with tallies and totals.
